summary: Defines the procedure used to update the IANA Language Subtag Registry in connection with the publication of RFC 5646. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The list of language name pieces needed refreshing. This explains how the list was brought up to date.

questions: how was the language subtag registry updated
what is the language subtag registry
how many language codes are there
subtitle: Adding thousands of language subtags to the international registry

tldr.problem: The Language Subtag Registry needed to include many more language codes from ISO standards that were unavailable when the previous version was created.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5646 defined a new version of the language tag syntax, and RFC 5645 documents the process and results of updating the registry to include approximately 7,500 new language subtags and seven new region subtags, plus deprecating old tags that could now be generated from new subtags.
tldr.outcome: The registry now includes comprehensive language code coverage from ISO 639-3 and 639-5, allowing more languages and language families to be tagged, while maintaining backward compatibility by marking obsolete tag patterns as deprecated.

today: RFC 5645 is an Informational RFC published in September 2009. It documents a complete replacement of the Language Subtag Registry contents and remains the reference for how that major update was carried out.

sections.title: The Language Subtag Registry
sections.content:
The Language Subtag Registry is a public list maintained by IANA that maps language codes to their names and properties. Tags like en for English, de for German, and fr for French are subtags. The registry also includes script codes (like Latn for Latin script) and region codes (like US for the United States).

RFC 5646 introduced a new version of the language tag standard that could support many more language codes. RFC 5645 describes the mechanical process of updating the registry to include these new codes, based on three ISO standards: ISO 639-3 (individual languages), ISO 639-5 (language families and groups), and ISO 3166-1 (region codes).
sections.eli5: Imagine a huge address book of language names and codes. When someone discovers a new language or invents a new way to name them, the book needs updating. This RFC explains how that was done.

sections.title: What Was Added and Changed
sections.content:
The update introduced approximately 7,500 new primary and extended language subtags drawn from ISO 639-3 and ISO 639-5. Primary subtags are for individual languages (like prs for Dari), and extended subtags build on them to distinguish varieties (for example, ar-nqf for a dialect of Arabic). The update also added seven new region subtags based on ISO 3166-1 exceptionally reserved code elements, and corrected capitalization and field ordering in thousands of existing entries.

The process involved merging entries from three ISO files: the ISO 639-3 language list with reference names, the ISO 639-3 name index showing all known names for each language, and the ISO 639-3 macrolanguage mappings that link dialect codes to their parent languages.
sections.eli5: The update added codes for thousands of previously uncovered languages and dialects, making the registry much more complete. It rearranged information to be clearer and more consistent.

sections.title: Macrolanguages, Sign Languages, and Scope
sections.content:
The registry distinguishes between individual languages and macrolanguages that encompass dialects. For example, Arabic (ar) is a macrolanguage that encompasses Modern Standard Arabic (arb), Gulf Arabic (afb), and other varieties. For languages that belong to a macrolanguage, a Macrolanguage field was added to the registry, showing which parent language they belong to.

Sign languages received special treatment: all sign language subtags were given an extended form with the prefix sgn, and old grandfathered sign language tags (like sgn-US for American Sign Language) were deprecated in favor of their modern equivalents (like ase).

The Scope field indicates whether a subtag represents an individual language, a macrolanguage, a language collection (from ISO 639-5), or a special use.
sections.eli5: Some language codes are for dialects that belong to a bigger language family, like how Spanish dialects belong to Spanish. The registry tracks these relationships. Sign languages also got special treatment to make them easier to identify.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility Through Deprecation
sections.content:
Old language tag combinations that were registered under RFC 1766 and RFC 3066 (like zh-hakka for Hakka Chinese) became redundant once the new codes existed. The RFC uses deprecation to manage this: the old tag is marked deprecated, but not removed, and points to its modern replacement via a Preferred-Value field. This lets old systems continue to recognize deprecated tags while new systems use the modern forms.

For example, zh-hakka was deprecated with Preferred-Value hak, because Hakka now has its own primary language code. Similarly, the old sign language tags like sgn-US, sgn-FR, and sgn-GB were deprecated in favor of their ISO 639-3 codes ase, fsl, and bfi respectively.
sections.eli5: When the registry added new, better codes for things that had old codes, it kept the old codes around but marked them as outdated, pointing to the new ones. That way, software expecting the old code can figure out what it should use instead.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content:
RFC 5645 is an Informational RFC documenting a one-time major update to the Language Subtag Registry. The registry itself is living: new subtags can be registered, and existing ones can be modified, according to the procedures defined in RFC 5646. The detailed contents of the registry that RFC 5645 describes are not included in the RFC itself; they live at the IANA website, where they are kept current as the registry evolves.

The registry is not a mirror of the underlying ISO standards; it is a curated list for use in language tags, with its own rules about which codes are included and how they are organized.
sections.eli5: This RFC explains the update but is not the actual list. The real list lives on the IANA website and keeps growing as new languages are added.
